title: Global Food Prices Hit Four-Year High as El Niño Fears and Black Sea Disruption Bite
excerpt: The FAO Food Price Index reached 136.0 in September, its highest since November 2022, as sugar hit an 18-month high and wheat futures a three-year peak.
body:
• The FAO Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points in September, up from 134.0 in August — the highest reading since November 2022.
  • El Niño fears pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while war-related Black Sea trade disruption sent wheat futures to a three-year peak.
  • FAO chief economist Máximo Torero warned that sustained pressure "will soon pass through to consumer food prices, especially in food and energy import-dependent countries."
  • The agency cut its 2026/27 world cereal trade forecast by 0.7%, citing lower wheat and maize exports as Black Sea shipping routes stay constrained.

World food prices climbed in September to their highest level in nearly four years, as logistics disruptions and weather worries tightened crop markets, the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization said Friday. The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in international prices for a basket of food commodities, averaged 136.0 points, up from a revised 134.0 for August — the highest reading since November 2022.

Benchmarks for cereals, sugar and vegetable oils all rose last month, though meat and dairy quotations fell. Fears about a severe El Niño weather pattern pushed international sugar prices to an 18-month high, while a war-related collapse in Black Sea trade pushed wheat futures to a three-year peak early last month, according to Reuters' reporting of the FAO data.

"We are seeing a persistent and increasingly broad-based build up in global commodity prices, as disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea combine with climate shocks, putting pressure on energy, transport and key food commodities."

— Máximo Torero, FAO Chief Economist

Two fronts: weather and war

On the weather front, the emerging El Niño threat has already unsettled sugar and palm-oil markets, with traders pricing in the risk of drought across Southeast Asia and erratic rainfall in Latin America. In August, extreme heat and drought across Europe had already hit prospects for the maize and sugar-beet harvests as well as livestock output. By September, the FAO said, cereal prices were being driven higher by the combination of those climate shocks and thinning trade flows.

On the geopolitical front, the picture is darker. Escalating attacks in the Black Sea have curtailed grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine in their four-and-a-half-year-old war, while the US–Iran conflict has strained flows of fertiliser for crops. FAO cut its forecast for world cereal trade in 2026/27 by 0.7% from September, citing lower wheat and maize export expectations due largely to constrained Black Sea shipping routes.

Why a big harvest isn't saving prices

The numbers carry a paradox. In a separate report released the same day, the FAO kept its forecast for global cereal production in 2026 almost unchanged at 2.979 billion metric tons — 2.1% below the previous year's peak, but still the second-largest harvest on record. Yet prices keep rising. Global totals say nothing about where grain is produced, whether it is the crop buyers need, or whether it can reach markets efficiently.

A large crop trapped behind disrupted shipping routes can coexist with shortages elsewhere, and strong production of one grain does not compensate for weak supplies of another. International markets exist to redistribute food from surplus regions to deficit regions — and when that mechanism slows, prices rise even when the world as a whole grows enough grain. Trade volumes matter as much as harvest totals.

The pass-through warning

Torero's warning was blunt: if sustained, the pressures "will soon pass through to consumer food prices, especially in food and energy import-dependent countries." The index remains nearly 17% below its record peak of March 2022, when Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent commodity markets reeling — but the direction of travel is unmistakable. August had already set the highest reading since late 2022, with the cereal index up 2.2% month-on-month to its highest since May 2024 and the vegetable-oil index at its highest since June 2022.

For households, the exposure is uneven. Import-dependent economies in Asia, the Middle East and Africa face the sharpest pass-through, and governments there are watching food-inflation prints that feed directly into subsidy bills and central-bank decisions. India, the world's largest importer of edible oils, sits squarely in the blast radius: palm and soybean oil prices feeding through to cooking-oil costs are a political as much as an economic variable.

What to watch

Three things will decide whether this turns into a durable food-price shock or a passing squeeze: whether El Niño arrives as a severe event or fizzles, whether Black Sea shipping stabilises or deteriorates further, and whether energy and fertiliser costs keep climbing alongside food commodities. The FAO releases its next index in early November. Between now and then, the wheat harvest in the southern hemisphere and the trajectory of the US–Iran confrontation will set the tone.
